g.text: Two numbers must change together, and they live on different machines
This is not a sharding problem. It is a 'make one node fast enough that you barely need to shard' problem.
One transfer, two shards, no single transaction
account A
account C
send $10
partition 3
partition 7
BEGIN ... COMMIT cannot span this
Debit succeeds, credit fails -> money has VANISHED
Credit succeeds, debit fails -> money has been CREATED, which is worse:
it is a mint, and it is unrecoverable
And unlike most systems you cannot resolve this by being
eventually consistent and moving on. A wallet is AUDITED -
someone will ask, months later, what a balance was on a
specific afternoon and why. 'Our reconciliation job fixed
the discrepancy' is not an answer to 'why'. That second,
independent constraint is what pushes this into event sourcing.
The requirement: 2,000,000 account updates/sec at peak
per-node write TPS
nodes needed
<- a typical managed RDBMS
<- the target
2,000 database nodes each holding a shard of the world's money -
each needing backups, failover, schema migrations, and participation
in distributed transactions - is not an architecture, it is an
operations disaster.
20 partitions
= 60 machines at RF 3
33x fewer, achieved by
changing the storage model,
not by buying hardware
Three ideas, each solving a problem the previous one exposes
1. Two local transactions, coordinated
No single transaction spans both shards, so the transfer
becomes debit-then-credit with a coordinator guaranteeing
both happen or neither's effect survives.
2. Store the CHANGES, not the balances
Instead of UPDATE balance = 90, append Debited(A, 10).
The balance becomes a FOLD over history - which is what
makes audit and reproducibility satisfiable, not approximable.
3. Only the event log must be reliable
Once balances are derived, state and snapshots are CACHES.
So durability concentrates on one append-only structure -
exactly the structure cheapest to make fast and to replicate.
The pleasing part is how the three requirements collapse into ONE mechanism. Correctness needs the two legs coordinated;
auditability needs history retained; throughput needs sequential writes. An append-only event log per shard, replicated by
consensus, delivers all three - and none of them individually would have forced that design.
IEEE-754 binary floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly. Accumulate that across a billion
transactions and balances drift with no bug to point at - the error is in the REPRESENTATION,
so every arithmetic operation contributes a little. Amounts are integer minor units, on the wire
as decimal strings. The most common correctness error in a money system, and entirely avoidable.
